# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
Sections 1–5 of this comment are a valuable correction to the Halden working paper. The attrition finding is new and important, and the record-based and actual-hours corrections are the right ones to make. Sections 6–8 overreach. The headline conclusion, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact", is not supported by the comment's own numbers. It is also contradicted by the randomised evidence the authors themselves call the most reliable in the literature.

## Arithmetic checks

Most figures reproduce:

| Figure | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Table 2, row 2 | 95.1 / 0.800 = 1.189 | +18.9% ✓ |
| Table 2, row 3 | 98.4 / 0.859 = 1.146 | +14.6% ✓ |
| Table 2, row 4 | 95.4 / 0.861 = 1.108 | +10.8% ✓ |
| Hours, 27 organisations | 34.6 / 40.3 | −14.1% ✓ |
| Hours, 17 organisations | 34.8 / 40.4 | −13.9% ✓ |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 | −2.6% ✓ |

Two figures do not reproduce:

1. **The hours decomposition (§3) doesn't add up.** Four days at 0.7 extra hours each, plus 1.6 hours logged on the day off, is 4.4 extra hours a week. Added to the 32 scheduled hours, that gives about 36.4 hours, or about 36.6 if the 0.7 is measured against baseline days of 8.06 hours. The reported figure is 34.6. To reach 34.6 with 1.6 hours on the day off, the four working days must have grown by only about 0.25 hours each. One of the two components is misstated.
2. **The novelty extrapolation (§6) doesn't give month ten.** A straight line through 0.61 SD at month 3 and 0.29 SD at month 6 falls by about 0.107 SD a month and reaches zero at about month **8.7**. An exponential decay never reaches zero. With only two points, neither the shape nor the date is identifiable.

## Strengths

- **Attrition (§1).** This is a substantive finding: the working paper misdescribed when and why organisations withdrew. Seven of the nine withdrew *after* the schedule began, and six of the nine cited workload or output. That makes the 61 a sample of survivors. (Six plus two accounts for eight of the nine; the ninth reason should be given.)
- **Manager versus record-based output (§2).** Of the 23 organisations that submitted records, the manager's index exceeded the record-based index in 19. That is a clean, direct test of rater bias, and it is presented fairly.
- **Hours (§3).** Logged hours replace an assumption. The finding of a 14% fall in actual hours closely parallels Varden's 13% in case processing.
- **Revenue (§4) and sectors (§5).** Both points are correct. Any output index above 80 mechanically shows a per-hour gain under a 20% hours cut, as I noted on the original paper.
- **Data note.** It is commendably candid. The problem is that the abstract and conclusion don't follow it (see point 3).

## Problems

### 1. The conclusion contradicts the best evidence the authors cite

The comment recommends record-based output, actual hours and a randomised comparison group. Varden's case-processing stratum has all three. It found output per actual hour up **12.5% (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)**, and its follow-up ran to nine months, beyond the month-six point at which the comment says the Halden gain was decaying.

The comment cites Varden's counter stratum as "the most reliable finding in the literature" but never mentions its case-processing stratum. Even in the counter stratum, output per hour rose by 6.7%, though that is plausibly a utilisation effect.

The comment's own corrected Halden estimate, +10.8%, is close to Varden's +12.5%. Two independent studies with different designs both arriving at roughly 11–12% is evidence *against* the gains being pure artifact. That remaining gain could be:

- a real effect;
- a novelty effect that persists beyond nine months;
- unlogged work that inflates the per-hour figure. Both studies flag this, and it would make the true gains smaller than measured.

But "entirely an artifact" is not established.

### 2. The abstract claims a correction that was never made

The abstract says that correcting "the first three" problems (attrition, output measure, hours) reduces the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. The withdrawn organisations are not in any of its rows. Attrition is identified but not quantified. The conclusion then counts it among the reasons the gain is artifact.

The two months of data the withdrawers produced could support a bounded or intention-to-treat estimate, for example by assigning them low output values. That would be worth doing, and it is the analysis the comment itself recommends.

### 3. Table 2 changes the sample as well as the correction

The four rows cover 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. The step from 23.4% to 10.8% therefore mixes correction effects with changes in which organisations are included.

- All four specifications should be computed within the same 17 organisations, so that each correction's contribution is isolated.
- The subsets also select for organisations with countable output and time tracking. That likely means work where output is more tied to hours.

The Data note acknowledges this. The abstract and conclusion nonetheless generalise to "reduced-hours schemes" as a whole.

### 4. The record-based measure may itself be biased downward

The submitted records include "billable hours delivered". Billable hours are an input measure. If they are used as output, a cut in hours shows up mechanically as a fall in output, regardless of what was actually produced. Organisations using billable hours should be reported separately, or excluded from the record-based index.

The manager index may also capture quality or other outputs that the records miss. That is not enough to overturn the 19-of-23 pattern, but the comment should not assume the records are the true value.

### 5. The novelty argument rests on the wrong variable

- **Energy is not output.** The comment uses a self-reported energy score with two data points as a stand-in for productivity decay.
- **The direct test is available but unreported.** Halden collected the output index *monthly*, and the comment has the microdata. It could show whether output per hour declined from month to month. If it did, that would be strong support for the novelty hypothesis. Not reporting it is a conspicuous gap.
- **The burden of proof applies both ways.** "Six months cannot distinguish novelty from a durable effect" supports "unproven". It does not support "entirely an artifact", which is a positive claim needing evidence of its own.

### 6. The meetings section mischaracterises Varden and applies a double standard

- **The data were not "selected for analysis after the results were known".** Varden says they were collected at managers' request in month six, during the trial. The analysis was unregistered, but that is not the same thing.
- **It is not a post hoc "subgroup".** Case processing was a pre-specified randomisation stratum.
- **Varden did not cite meetings as a mechanism.** Varden stated that seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism" and registered a confirmatory test. The comment's advice that the hypothesis "should not be cited as a mechanism" agrees with Varden's own position, but is presented as a rebuttal.
- **Double standard.** The comment rejects Varden's unregistered exploratory result, but relies on an unregistered two-point self-report trend for its own novelty claim.
- **Confusing "not rest" with "not real".** If the gain comes from cutting low-value meetings, it is a real efficiency gain, not a measurement artifact. Such a gain could also be achieved *without* cutting hours. That is an important policy point, but it is a different conclusion from the one the comment draws. Halden's managers also cited meeting cuts (47 of 58), so the hypothesis has support in both studies.

### 7. Smaller points

- **Deflator.** CPI is not the right deflator for organisations' revenue. Sector output price indices would be better. And without a comparison group, a real fall of 2.6% cannot be attributed to the pilot, by the same reasoning the comment applies elsewhere.
- **Retail sample.** The retail figure of −11.2% rests on three organisations. Its similarity to Varden's counter result (−11.4%) is suggestive, but the sample is too small to stand alone.
- **Sector conclusion.** "Where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output" is well supported, mainly by Varden.

## A conclusion the evidence supports

> The Halden pilot's 23.4% gain in output per hour is substantially overstated. Correcting for manager-rated output and scheduled hours, in a non-random subset of surviving organisations, reduces it to about 11%. Non-random attrition, not yet quantified, would likely reduce it further. This residual is similar to the 12.5% found in Varden's randomised case-processing stratum. Whether such gains persist beyond nine months, and how much of them reflects removed low-value time rather than rest, remains open. Where output depends on staff presence, reduced hours reduce output.

## Across the three documents

Read together, the three documents point to a consistent picture:

- Halden's headline figures are inflated by its design.
- In work not tied to presence, carefully measured per-hour gains of roughly 10–13% appear in both studies.
- Coverage-bound work loses output.
- Durability over time and the mechanism behind the gains are unresolved.

The comment strengthens the first point substantially but argues past the second.

I can draft a referee report on the comment, or set out the same-sample re-analysis of Table 2 and the month-by-month output test as concrete requests to the authors.
